questions.problem: Find the integral of $\frac{2}{x}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ with respect to $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{2}{x}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}})\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x-\int {x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{{x}^{-1/2+1}}{(-\frac{1}{2}+1)}+C \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-2{x}^{1/2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we apply the sum and constant factor rules and take the coefficients out of the integral. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{10}{x}-\sqrt[3]{x})\text{d}x & =10\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x-\int {x}^{1/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{{x}^{1/3+1}}{(\frac{1}{3}+1)}+C \\  & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{3}{4}{x}^{4/3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=10\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{10}{x}-\sqrt[3]{x})\text{d}x & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}}+10\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =10(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K)-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}} \\  & =10\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{{x}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1-\frac{2}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (1-\frac{4}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x-\int \frac{4}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{4}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+4\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+4\cdot \frac{{x}^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+C \\  & =x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{4}{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-4\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1-\frac{2}{x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{4}{x}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-4\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =x-\frac{4}{x}-4(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =x-\frac{4}{x}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the integral of $\dfrac 1 {2x} + 3x$ with respect to $x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{1}{2x}+3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x+\int 3x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+3\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+3\cdot \frac{{x}^{1+1}}{1+1}+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|}{2}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

                    Integrating a Reciprocal Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+\frac{2x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{3}{x}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+2\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C =3 \ln K$ where $K$ is some other constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $3\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3+2x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2x+C \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2x+3\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|)+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that for $x >0,$ we have 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\ln{x}) = \dfrac 1 x.
$$

We can generalize this to all values $x\neq 0$ by including an absolute value inside the natural logarithm: 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\ln{|x|}) = \dfrac 1 x.
$$

Therefore, the integral of the reciprocal function is

$$
\int \dfrac 1 x \,\textrm{d}x = \ln |x| + C.
$$

tutorials.name: Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms
tutorials.problem:
For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C = \ln K,$ where $K>0$ is some other constant. Then, using the laws of logarithms, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$
